rows.statement: Alligator arms: A receiver who will not extend his arms for a catch for fear of contact; also called T-rex arms.

sources.citation: NFL draft glossary: Fluid hips, cow on ice and more (ESPN)
sources.quote: a specimen who won't extend his arms for a catch for fear of injury

rows.statement: analyst: A support-staff member who studies film or data for a team; titles include recruiting analyst (college) and data analyst (NFL).

sources.citation: College Football Staffs Are Growing: The Careers Behind Today's Modern Programs (Sports Management Worldwide)

rows.statement: Anchor: A lineman's ability to stand his ground and not be moved back, especially against a bull rush.

sources.quote: Used to describe a lineman’s ability to stand and hold his ground and not be moved.

sources.citation: Todd McShay's guide to every combine drill (ESPN)

sources.citation: From Camp Body to Big Bubble to Wood-Toter's Ass: A Scouting Terms Glossary (Defector)

rows.statement: Angle block (down block): A block made on a defender from an angle, not head-on (often a down block toward the inside).

sources.quote: Angle/Down Block – Simple block where a blocker blocks a defensive player from an angle, not head on.

rows.notes: Only Steelers Depot found. Flag: single publisher.

rows.statement: Anticipation: Throwing or reacting before the play shows itself, such as a quarterback releasing the ball before the receiver comes out of his break.

sources.citation: PFF QB Evaluation: what we look for on tape (PFF)
sources.quote: Whether it’s anticipating a window or a receiver coming out of his his break

sources.citation: Scout Series Pt. 6: Quarterbacks - What Scouts Look for (NFL Draft Diamonds)
sources.quote: process fast, throw with anticipation

sources.citation: The NFL Draft Scouting Glossary (The Ringer)
sources.quote: struggled to read defenses and throw with anticipation

rows.statement: area scout: A scout who covers a specific geographic area of the country or specific conferences, visiting schools and writing reports on prospects.

sources.quote: area scouts -- those who cover a specific geographical area of the country or specific conferences

rows.statement: Arm talent: A quarterback's overall throwing ability: arm strength, quick release, accuracy, touch and the ability to throw from different platforms.

sources.quote: Arm talent can be grouped into a bucket of accuracy, arm strength, the ability to pace and layer the ball

rows.notes: Single publisher (PFF). Bleacher Report grades 'arm strength' separately; the draft's 'raw ability to make throws' was widened by PFF to include accuracy.

rows.statement: assistant general manager: A deputy to the general manager; the NFL media policy treats the title as a 'secondary football executive' who is next in line to the top football executive and supervises player personnel.

sources.citation: Chiefs Front Office Staff (NFL (Kansas City Chiefs club site))
sources.quote: ASSISTANT GENERAL MANAGER

rows.notes: Both sources are NFL properties (one publisher). College programs also use the title (SMWW).

rows.statement: AT spotter: A certified athletic trainer in the stadium booth who watches for injuries and can call for a player to be examined.

sources.citation: Concussion Protocol & Return-to-Participation Protocol: Overview (NFL)

rows.notes: NFL pages call the role 'booth ATC spotter'; rulebook says 'AT Spotter'. The 'certified' reading of ATC is not spelled out in the opened text. Two sources.

sources.quote: shortened huddles and huddling much closer to the line of scrimmage than usual.

rows.notes: Single source (Wikipedia hurry-up offense page, per the retrieved summary); the Bengals 1988 attribution was in the draft and the page excerpt did not quote it.

rows.statement: Audible: A play change the quarterback calls at the line of scrimmage after seeing the defense, replacing the play called in the huddle.

sources.citation: Glossary of American football terms - Wikipedia (Wikipedia)
American Football Terms Glossary | Under Armour (Under Armour (UA Playbooks))

sources.quote: When the offense or defense decides their play at the line of scrimmage rather than in the huddle.

rows.statement: B gap: The gap between an offensive guard and tackle.

sources.citation: Gap (American football) (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: A gap between the offensive guard and tackle is called a "B" gap.

sources.quote: The area between the Guard and Tackle

sources.quote: Between the guard and tackle

sources.quote: the next gap (between guard and tackle) labeled as the “B” gap

sources.quote: The gap between the guard and tackle.

rows.notes: Viqtory and Lance Reisland call the tackle/tight-end gap the C gap; Wikipedia calls every gap outside the tackle a C gap. | Other batch definition: The gap between a guard and a tackle.

rows.statement: Back-shoulder fade: A fade thrown behind or to the back shoulder of the receiver, away from the defender, usually against man coverage.

sources.quote: The "back-shoulder fade" (ball thrown behind the receiver or to the back shoulder versus man coverage)

rows.notes: Only Bleacher Report found. Flag: single publisher.

rows.statement: Backed up: An offense starting a possession or a down near its own goal line, with little room behind it.

sources.citation: Glossary of Football Terms (ACTIVE.com)
sources.quote: the offense has to start backed up by its own end zone.

sources.citation: 28 Football Terms to Make You Sound Like a Pro (Dictionary.com)

rows.notes: Only used descriptively in sources (coffin-corner entries); no glossary defines 'backed up' itself. Weak.

rows.statement: Backfield: The area behind the line of scrimmage, and the offensive players (quarterback and backs) who line up there.

sources.citation: NFL Football Operations | Football Terms (NFL Football Operations)
sources.quote: Offensive Backfield: The area behind the offensive line where the quarterback and running backs line up.

sources.citation: American Football Terms Glossary | Under Armour (Under Armour (UA Playbooks))
sources.quote: Backfield: The offensive players behind the line of scrimmage, specifically, the quarterback and running back.

sources.citation: Glossary of American football terms - Wikipedia (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: The area of an American football field behind the line of scrimmage.

sources.citation: Glossary of American football (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: The area of an American football field behind the line of scrimmage.

rows.notes: Other batch definition: The area behind the line of scrimmage, and the offensive players (quarterback, running backs, fullback) who line up there.

rows.statement: bail: A corner's technique of turning and sinking backward at the snap, often from a press alignment, to get depth for the deep zone.

sources.citation: NFL 101: Breaking Down the Basics of the Zone Blitz (Bleacher Report)
sources.quote: a “bail” technique (sink, stack on top of the receiver)

rows.notes: One publisher.

rows.statement: Ball placement: Putting the pass where only the receiver can get it and where he can keep running, such as the outside shoulder or in stride.

sources.citation: A Scout's Guide to Grading Quarterbacks (Bleacher Report)
sources.quote: we are looking for ball placement and control of the football

sources.citation: Scout Series Pt. 6: Quarterbacks - What Scouts Look for (NFL Draft Diamonds)
sources.quote: it’s ball placement. Can he throw to a receiver’s leverage?

rows.statement: Ball skills: A defender's or receiver's ability to find, track and play the ball in the air, including high-pointing and making interceptions or catches.

sources.quote: displayed high-level ball skills down the field

sources.quote: Speed is the foundation on which coverage ability and ball skills are built.

sources.quote: This type of defensive player has outstanding instincts in the passing game, leading to interceptions and pass breakups.

sources.quote: The ability to find and track the ball when thrown.

rows.statement: Bandit: A hybrid defensive end/linebacker rush role used by some defenses, mostly in college; the label is a team playbook name, not one fixed position.

sources.quote: Bandit is a defensive playbook name, not one standard college position.

sources.citation: Why defensive players have the coolest position names in college football (ESPN)
Linebacker (Wikipedia) (Wikipedia)

rows.notes: At West Virginia in the early 2000s bandits were safeties (ESPN, via summariser), so the meaning varies by program.

rows.statement: banjo: A man-coverage call used against stacked, bunched or slot receivers in which defenders switch assignments by what the receivers do.

sources.citation: Fantasy shells: coverage glossary (Fantasy Points)
sources.quote: Used by secondaries to counter stacked, bunched receiver formations, and spread offenses

rows.notes: One publisher. Mechanics (switching by routes) from the draft are not confirmed by a second page.

rows.statement: Base block: A solo block by an offensive lineman, squared up to the defender.

sources.citation: Kozora football terminology glossary (Steelers Depot)
sources.quote: Solo block by an offensive lineman. Square to the defender.

rows.notes: Single source (Kozora glossary).

rows.notes: Only one publisher (Wikipedia) found; the page names Sean McDermott's teams and TCU as examples. Flag: single publisher.

rows.notes: College rules not checked. Rulebook only.

rows.notes: One publisher. Draft said 'two-gap technique'; not supported.

sources.citation: What Exactly Does Each Member of an NFL Team's Front Office Do? (Bleacher Report)
sources.quote: scouting other teams is typically delegated amongst a number of league scouts under the team's employ

rows.notes: Bleacher Report heads this section 'Director of Pro Personnel' but its text calls the job 'director of player personnel'. The draft's 'director of pro scouting' title was not found. Single publisher; flagged.

rows.statement: director of recruiting: A staff executive who leads a college program's recruiting department.

sources.citation: College Football Staffs Are Growing: The Careers Behind Today's Modern Programs (Sports Management Worldwide)
sources.quote: major programs now employ recruiting directors, personnel evaluators, high school relations staff

rows.notes: Weak, single publisher: sources read do not define the title. Flagged.

rows.statement: disguise: Showing a coverage look before the snap that differs from the coverage actually played.

sources.citation: ITP Glossary: Cover 3 (Inside the Pylon / Scouting Academy)
sources.quote: show Cover 4 before the snap, but roll their coverage to Cover 3 as the play begins

rows.notes: Single publisher.

rows.statement: Dive: A quick handoff to a back attacking straight ahead into the interior of the defense.

sources.citation: Glossary of American football terms - Wikipedia (Wikipedia)
Option offense - Wikipedia (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: This quick surge into the interior of the defense is traditionally called a "dive".

sources.citation: American football plays - Wikipedia (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: Also called dive, plunge, buck, gut, slam or numerous other names.

rows.notes: Wikipedia only (three pages).

rows.statement: Divide routes: Any route combination designed to stress the safety.

sources.citation: Kozora football terminology glossary (Steelers Depot, 2013) (Steelers Depot)
sources.quote: Divide Routes – Any route combination designed to stress the safety.

rows.notes: Draft's example (go and post) is not in the quote; removed. Flag: single publisher.

rows.statement: Dog: West Coast playbook word for a blitz.

sources.citation: West Coast Offense Definition and Pass Protection Terminology (Queer Football Breakdowns) (Queer Football Breakdowns)
sources.quote: blitz is called "dog" in the playbook

rows.notes: Only one source found. Flag: single publisher.

rows.statement: Double out: A route in which the receiver runs 5 to 8 yards, cuts outside, and then turns vertically upfield.

sources.citation: Route (gridiron football) - Wikipedia (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: A double out is when a receiver runs 5-8 yards down field cuts outside, then cuts vertically upfield

rows.notes: Single source with an odd description (the page text appears to describe an out-and-up); flagged for a second source.

rows.statement: Double reverse: A play in which the ball reverses direction twice behind the line of scrimmage, usually with two or three handoffs.

sources.citation: Glossary of American football (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: A play in which the ball reverses direction twice behind the line of scrimmage

rows.notes: Only Wikipedia found. Flag: single publisher.

rows.statement: Double slot: A formation with two slot receivers inside two outside receivers (a four-receiver look), as in the air raid and run and shoot.

sources.citation: Air raid offense - Wikipedia (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: The formations often feature two outside receivers and two inside slot receivers.

sources.citation: Spread offense - Wikipedia (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: evolved into a double-slot formation

rows.notes: Wikipedia only; the page does not use the exact term double slot for the air raid sentence.

rows.statement: Double team: Two blockers engage one defender together, often before one climbs to the next level.

sources.citation: Glossary of American football (block entry) (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: double-team block, where two blockers simultaneously block one player

sources.citation: Breaking down PFF's run concepts (PFF)
sources.quote: they’ll look to double team, if possible, before finding their predetermined second-level assignment

sources.citation: Inside look at the NFL's most popular run blocking concepts (Nick Shook) (NFL)
sources.quote: the playside guard blocks down in either a double team on a nose or directly on a backside linebacker

rows.statement: Double wing: A formation with two tight ends and two wingbacks in which the snap goes to a quarterback or halfback moderately deep in the backfield.

sources.citation: Glossary of American football terms - Wikipedia (Wikipedia)

rows.notes: Level set to college: nothing in the sources puts it in the NFL.

rows.statement: Downhill runner: A back who attacks upfield quickly with forward lean and no sideways hesitation (north-south runner).

sources.citation: The NFL Draft Scouting Glossary (The Ringer)
sources.quote: There’s no dancing at the line of scrimmage. There’s no hesitation.

sources.citation: NFL draft glossary: Fluid hips, cow on ice and more (ESPN)
sources.quote: A ball carrier who can power through tackles while almost falling forward

sources.citation: 2018 Scouting Glossary (Draft Insiders)
sources.quote: Back with good body lean who attacks the line of scrimmage quickly.

rows.notes: Mayock's 'downhill thumper' is a different usage for a physical linebacker.

rows.statement: Downing a punt: The coverage team touches or stops the punt so the play ends without a return.

sources.citation: CFBTrack: College Football Special Teams Glossary (CFBTrack)
sources.quote: A punt touched or stopped by the kicking team to end the play without a return.

sources.citation: Wikipedia: Punt (gridiron football) (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: is often said to have 'downed the ball' when this occurs

rows.notes: Draft alias 'pin' unsourced. NFL rule 9-2-2 first-touching rules let the kicking team touch a punt beyond the line only after the receivers have touched it, or the receivers may take it at that spot (R).

rows.statement: Drag: A shallow crossing route over the middle that starts very short and may drift deeper across the field.

sources.citation: Route (gridiron football) (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: A drag route (also known as an in route or a dig route) is a route run by a receiver

sources.citation: The Complete Guide to Football Routes (Throw Deep Publishing) (Throw Deep Publishing)
sources.quote: The drag route is a horizontal route that starts off very short

rows.notes: Wikipedia gives drag as another name for an in/dig route; Throw Deep describes a shallow horizontal route. Two publishers.

rows.statement: Draw: A run disguised as a pass: the quarterback drops back, then hands off to a back or keeps it.

sources.citation: Glossary of American football terms - Wikipedia (Wikipedia)
American Football Terms Glossary | Under Armour (Under Armour (UA Playbooks))
sources.quote: Draw: An offensive play where the quarterback drops back to act like they're passing

sources.citation: American football plays - Wikipedia (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: In a draw play, the offensive line drops into pass blocking positions

sources.citation: Glossary of American football (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: A play in which the quarterback drops back as if to pass, then hands off to a running back

rows.notes: Other batch definition: A run disguised as a pass: the line pass-blocks and the quarterback fakes a drop before handing off (or keeping).

rows.statement: Drive success rate: The share of drives on which the offense either gains a first down or scores.

sources.citation: NFL Team Stat Explorer Glossary (4for4)
sources.quote: percent of drives in which the offense either gained a first down or scored

sources.citation: Football Outsiders - Wikipedia (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: Drive Stats calculate a team's average success rate on a possession-by-possession basis

rows.notes: Draft name 'Series success rate' was not found; 4for4 calls it 'Drive Success %'.

rows.statement: Durability: How likely a player is to stay healthy and available; scouts and coaches mark injury-prone players down.

sources.citation: Draft lingo is a special language (Fox Sports)
sources.quote: You’ll often hear coaches or scouts say this privately about injury-prone or constantly injured players.

sources.citation: B/R NFL 1,000: A Scout's Guide to Grading Wide Receivers (Bleacher Report)
sources.quote: Not only looking at actual injuries, but time missed to injury.

rows.notes: Two usages, neither a definition of the word 'durability'.

rows.statement: DVOA: Football Outsiders' rating of how much better or worse a team or unit is than league average on each play, adjusted for down and distance and opponent strength.

sources.citation: Football Outsiders - Wikipedia (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: DVOA (Defense-adjusted Value Over Average) calculates a team's success based on the down-and-distance of each play during the season

sources.citation: A Guide to Modern Football Analytics for Beginners (New England Patriots)
sources.quote: DVOA measures a team's efficiency by comparing success on every single play to a league average based on situation and

sources.citation: Betting 101: Explaining Commonly Cited Metrics and Factors in our Handicapping (PFF)
sources.quote: DVOA, or Defense-adjusted Value Over Expected, is a scaled metric of each team's performance relative to the opposition.

sources.citation: Football Outsiders Stats Explainer (ESPN)
sources.quote: DVOA (defense-adjusted value over average), breaks down the entire season play by play.

rows.notes: PFF spells it 'Value Over Expected'; the other three say 'Over Average'. Football Outsiders shut down in 2023 and DVOA moved to FTN Fantasy (Wikipedia).

rows.statement: DYAR: A player's total value above a replacement-level player, expressed in yards, over a season rather than per play.

sources.citation: Football Outsiders - Wikipedia (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: DYAR (Defense-adjusted Yards Above Replacement) calculates each player's cumulative value above or below a "replacement-level" alternative.

sources.citation: Football Outsiders Stats Explainer (ESPN)
sources.quote: Defense-adjusted Yards Above Replacement.

rows.notes: ESPN's explainer also says DYAR translates success into the yards it is worth. Two publishers only.

rows.statement: Dynamic kickoff: The NFL kickoff format, adopted in 2024, in which the kicker is the only kicking-team player behind the 40 and the receiving team sets up in a defined setup zone, with most players held still until the ball lands, so the play looks more like a scrimmage play.

sources.citation: 2024 NFL Season: Explaining rules for new dynamic kickoff (NFL)
sources.quote: The rules are designed to promote more kickoff returns.

sources.citation: NFL Rulebook 2026 (NFL Rulebook)
sources.quote: the restraining line for the remaining 10 players of the kicking team shall be the receiving team’s 40-yard line

sources.citation: Wikipedia: Kickoff (gridiron football) (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: one or two returners are allowed in the "landing zone" between the goal line and the 20

rows.notes: NFL.com (2024) and the 2026 rulebook differ on details: NFL.com says seven receivers on the restraining line and a 30-yard touchback; the 2026 rulebook (6-1-3, 6-1-5) requires at least five and uses 20 or 35. The 2026 rulebook supersedes. NFL.com says 2024 onside kicks were limited to the fourth quarter; 2026 rule 6-1-6 allows a declared onside kick any time.

rows.statement: Eagle front: A 3-4 one-gap front where both ends align in a 4i (inside shoulder of the tackle) and play the B gap, the nose works to the front side A gap, and the Sam plays a two-gap technique over the tight end.

sources.citation: NFL 101: The Basics of the 3-4 Defensive Front (Bleacher Report)
sources.quote: both defensive ends (E) align in a “4i” (inside shoulder of the tackle) and play the B-gap

rows.notes: Bowen: Steelers, Packers and Redskins ran it. One publisher. Draft said alignments 'vary by coach' with no detail; replaced by the sourced Bowen version.

rows.statement: early enrollee: A recruit who enrolls before the fall semester, often in January, to join the program early.

sources.citation: College Football Recruiting & Roster Glossary (CFBTrack)
sources.quote: A recruit who enrolls before the fall semester, often in January, to join the program early.

rows.notes: Draft wording 'before his senior spring ends' not in any source; removed. Single publisher; flagged.

rows.statement: Early entrant: A college player who enters the NFL draft before using up his college eligibility, with league approval.

sources.citation: NFL Draft Rules (NFL)
sources.quote: may request the league's approval to enter the draft early

sources.citation: Forty-two players granted special eligibility for 2026 NFL Draft (NFL)
sources.quote: renounced their college football eligibility by submitting written notification to the league office

rows.notes: NFL.com's announcement lists 42 players with special eligibility and 21 more whose degrees are complete; the second group needs no petition.

rows.statement: early signing period: A signing window before the traditional February date that lets recruits formalize their choice in December (the 2025 cycle began Dec. 4, 2024).

sources.citation: NCAA approves elimination of national letter of intent program (ESPN)
sources.quote: The early signing period for the 2025 cycle starts Dec. 4, 2024

sources.citation: College Football Recruiting & Roster Glossary (CFBTrack)
sources.quote: An earlier signing window that allows recruits to formalize their college choice before the traditional signing date.

rows.notes: Draft said 'three-day window'; the length is not stated in sources read, removed. ESPN also notes commissioners declined a formal vote on a June signing period.

rows.statement: edge rusher: A defender whose main job is attacking the quarterback from the outside edge of the offensive line: a defensive end in a four-man front or an outside linebacker in a three-man front.

sources.citation: Glossary of American football terms (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: A defensive player whose most common role is attacking the quarterback from the edge of the offensive line.

sources.citation: NFL 101: The Basics of the 3-4 Defensive Front (Bleacher Report)
sources.quote: make plays as edge defenders out of a stand-up, two-point stance

sources.citation: Linebacker (Wikipedia) (Wikipedia)

rows.notes: Wikipedia Linebacker page (via summariser) describes the 3-4 outside linebacker as lining up in front of the tackles like a true defensive end and rushing the passer.

rows.statement: eight in the box: Eight defenders in the box, which happens when a safety moves down to help against the run.

sources.citation: Formation (American football) (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: "8 in the box" is used to indicate that one of the two safeties has moved into the box

sources.citation: Understanding Football with Joel Klatt: Breaking down defensive coverages (FOX Sports)
sources.quote: you have one more player than the offense can block

rows.statement: eligibility waiver: An NCAA-granted exception that excuses an athlete from an eligibility rule, such as a waiver for immediate eligibility after a transfer; most categories are eliminated for D-I and D-II from 2026-27.

sources.citation: What is the NCAA transfer portal? Everything you need to know (On3)
sources.quote: unless they obtained a special eligibility waiver from the NCAA.

sources.citation: Division I and II Age-Based Eligibility Rules (Eligibility 101) (NCAA)
sources.quote: Included multiple waiver options

rows.notes: Draft said 'a school's request'; sources show the NCAA grants it. Historical for most uses. Two publishers.

rows.statement: Empty backfield: A formation with no running back in the backfield with the quarterback, so every other eligible receiver is split out or on the line.

sources.citation: Breaking down NFL offensive personnel groupings (Bleacher Report)
sources.quote: there's little else to do with no backs in the backfield besides throw the ball.

sources.citation: A pro-style formation system (Queer Football Breakdowns)
sources.quote: To put the HB out wide to make empty formations

rows.notes: 'All five eligible receivers' in the draft is inferred from the five-eligible rule; not worded that way in sources.

rows.statement: End around: A play where a receiver motions into the backfield, takes a direct handoff from the quarterback and runs around the opposite end; often confused with a reverse.

sources.citation: Glossary of American football terms - Wikipedia (Wikipedia)

rows.notes: Single source. Wikipedia glossary says a reverse differs in that a back first carries one way and hands to a receiver going the other way.

rows.statement: equipment manager: The staff member who runs a team's equipment room.

sources.citation: Chiefs Front Office Staff (NFL (Kansas City Chiefs club site))
sources.quote: Equipment Director

sources.citation: College Football Staffs Are Growing: The Careers Behind Today's Modern Programs (Sports Management Worldwide)
sources.quote: Equipment

rows.notes: Titles only; no source defines the job. Flagged.

rows.statement: Erhardt-Perkins offense: A play-calling system that names plays by concept and formation rather than by route numbers, so players learn tasks from their starting alignment.

sources.citation: Play calling system (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: the Erhardt–Perkins system is based on loose "concepts" that adapt to a variety of personnel packages and formations.

sources.citation: Speak My Language (Chris B. Brown, Grantland) (Grantland)
sources.quote: New England's offense is a member of the NFL's third offensive family, the Erhardt-Perkins system.

rows.notes: Two publishers.

rows.statement: evaluation period: A recruiting-calendar period when coaches may watch a recruit play or visit his school, but may not speak with him or his parents in person off campus.

sources.citation: College football recruiting calendar: Key dates for NCAA cycle (Sports Illustrated)
sources.quote: Coaches cannot speak directly with prospects or their parents off the college campus, but can watch athletes from the stands

sources.citation: Glossary of Recruiting Terms (ACTIVE.com)
sources.quote: In-person, off-campus recruiting contact during evaluations is prohibited.

sources.citation: College Football Recruiting & Roster Glossary (CFBTrack)
sources.quote: A recruiting period when coaches may evaluate prospects, such as at games, practices, or events.

rows.statement: Even front: A 4-3 base look with no nose tackle, a left and right tackle instead.

sources.citation: 4-3 defense (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: there is a left and right defensive tackle

rows.notes: Single publisher. Fetch-tool paraphrase of Wikipedia's 4-3 article.

rows.statement: Expected points: The average points the team with the ball can expect to score next, given down, distance, field position and time remaining.

sources.citation: Expected points and EPA explained (ESPN)
sources.quote: assigns an "expected points" value to the team with the ball at the start of each play based on the

sources.citation: How is Total QBR calculated? We explain our quarterback rating (ESPN)
sources.quote: This estimate is known as "expected points."

sources.citation: Betting 101: Explaining Commonly Cited Metrics and Factors in our Handicapping (PFF)
sources.quote: Expected points is an estimate of how many points a team will score on a drive, given the current situation

sources.citation: A Guide to Modern Football Analytics for Beginners (New England Patriots)
sources.quote: to define how many points a player or play is worth to a team.

rows.notes: ESPN counts points until the score changes or the half ends; PFF describes it per drive. Minor model differences.

rows.statement: Expected points added: The change in expected points from the start of a play to the start of the next, used to value each play.

sources.citation: Expected points and EPA explained (ESPN)
sources.quote: This difference in EP from one play to the next is called expected points added (EPA).

sources.citation: Betting 101: Explaining Commonly Cited Metrics and Factors in our Handicapping (PFF)
sources.quote: EPA is the difference in Expected Points before and after each play.

sources.citation: How is Total QBR calculated? We explain our quarterback rating (ESPN)
sources.quote: That change in the expected points caused by the outcome of the play represents the play’s value

sources.citation: Football analytics definitions (Sumer Sports)
sources.quote: Average Expected Points Added per offensive play.

rows.notes: Sumer's entry is for 'EPA per Play'.

rows.statement: Explosive play: A run or pass that gains a large chunk of yards; the cutoff varies (commonly 10 or more on runs, 15 or more on passes).

sources.citation: NFL Team Stat Explorer Glossary (4for4)
sources.quote: percent of passing plays that gain at least 15 yards

sources.citation: Football analytics definitions (Sumer Sports)
sources.quote: The share of pass attempts that result in a gain of 15 or more yards.

sources.citation: PFF Signature Statistics - a glossary (PFF)
sources.quote: we classify any run of 15 or more yards as a breakaway run.

rows.notes: Threshold is not standard across sources.

rows.statement: Extra gear: A top speed or burst a player shows only when he needs it, so he pulls away from coverage after seeming to have reached his limit.

sources.citation: The NFL Draft Scouting Glossary (The Ringer)
sources.quote: he slams on the afterburners and runs away from coverage

sources.citation: NFL draft glossary: Fluid hips, cow on ice and more (ESPN)
sources.quote: The fastest possible speed.

rows.statement: Extra point: The one-point kick after a touchdown, snapped from the 15-yard line in the NFL (a kick of about 33 yards); in college the try is snapped from the 3-yard line.

sources.citation: NFL Football Operations: Football Terms (NFL)
sources.quote: snapped from the 15-yardline for the attempt and the kick is equivalent to about a 33-yard field goal

sources.citation: NFL Rulebook 2026 (NFL Rulebook)
sources.quote: 15 yards from the defensive team’s goal line for a Try kick

sources.citation: American Football Terms Glossary (UA Playbooks) (Under Armour)
sources.quote: A scoring play that happens after a touchdown worth one point

sources.citation: NCAA Football Rules and Interpretations 2026 (NCAA Rulebook)
sources.quote: A try is an opportunity for either team to score one or two points

sources.citation: 28 Football Terms to Make You Sound Like a Pro (Dictionary.com)
sources.quote: Stands for "point after touchdown", also known as "an extra point."

rows.notes: Merged the draft's 'PAT distance' row. NFL rulebook calls it a Try kick (11-3). The NCAA 3-yard spot is from Rule 8-3-2 (snap on the opponent's three-yard line or farther back). The NCAA rulebook uses 'try', not 'extra point', for the whole play.

rows.statement: Eyes: Where a quarterback or defender looks; quarterbacks use their eyes to read the field or to manipulate safeties, and keeping eyes up under pressure is a plus.

sources.citation: PFF QB Evaluation: what we look for on tape (PFF)
sources.quote: All of the elite players are able to play with their eyes up

sources.citation: Scout Series Pt. 6: Quarterbacks - What Scouts Look for (NFL Draft Diamonds)
sources.quote: manipulate safeties with their eyes

rows.notes: Fox (2014) mocks Mayock's phrase 'eye discipline'; no sentence defines it.

rows.statement: F (F-back): A flexible letter for the fourth skill player: the fullback in two-back sets, or the second tight end in one-back sets with two tight ends.

sources.citation: A pro-style formation system (Queer Football Breakdowns)
sources.quote: In two-back formations, this is the fullback, and in one-back sets with two TE's, this is the second TE.

rows.notes: Single source describing one pro-style letter system.

rows.statement: Fade: A vertical route down the sideline in which the receiver tries to get on top of the defender, often with a ball thrown to the outside or back shoulder.

sources.citation: NFL 101: Breaking Down the Basics of the Route Tree (Bleacher Report)
sources.quote: The fade route can be identified with multiple terminology (go, fly, clear-out, etc.).

sources.citation: Route (gridiron football) - Wikipedia (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: When run down the sidelines, a fly can be called a fade route.

sources.citation: Understanding The Route Tree In Football (vIQtory Sports)
sources.quote: The fade route is also known as a seam route, streak route, and a 9 route.

rows.notes: Viqtory calls the fade a seam route too, but Throw Deep and Bleacher Report describe the seam as a separate route up the middle.

rows.statement: Fake field goal: A play from field goal formation in which the holder or kicker runs or throws instead of kicking.

sources.citation: CFBTrack: College Football Special Teams Glossary (CFBTrack)
sources.quote: A play where the kicking team lines up for a field goal but runs or passes instead.

sources.citation: Wikipedia: Punter (gridiron football) (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: Punters may pass or run the ball on fake field goal attempts and fake punts.

rows.notes: Two publishers.

rows.statement: Fake punt: A play from punt formation in which a player other than the punter runs or throws instead of kicking.

sources.citation: Wikipedia: Punt (gridiron football) (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: a punting team will elect to attempt a 'fake punt'—line up in punt formation and begin the process as normal

sources.citation: CFBTrack: College Football Special Teams Glossary (CFBTrack)
sources.quote: A play where the punting team pretends to punt but runs or passes instead.

rows.notes: Two publishers (Wikipedia and CFBTrack); the Wikipedia positions page also notes upbacks may take the snap on fakes.

rows.statement: FBS: The Football Bowl Subdivision, the top level of college football, whose teams play in the College Football Playoff and other bowl games.

sources.citation: NCAA Division I Athletics, Scholarships & Championships (NCAA)
sources.quote: The Football Bowl Subdivision is the highest level of Division I football

sources.citation: NCAA Division I Football Bowl Subdivision (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: is the highest level of college football in the United States.

sources.citation: Glossary of American football (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: Historically known as Division I-A.

rows.notes: 138 teams in 2026 per Wikipedia.

rows.statement: FCS: The Football Championship Subdivision, the second level of Division I football, with limited scholarships and its own NCAA playoff.

sources.citation: NCAA Division I Athletics, Scholarships & Championships (NCAA)
sources.quote: FCS teams play in a separate single-elimination playoff tournament.

sources.citation: NCAA Division I Football Championship Subdivision (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: is the second-highest level of college football in the United States

sources.citation: Glossary of American football (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: Distinguished from FBS by reduced scholarship limits and the existence of an official NCAA championship event.

rows.notes: 128 teams in 2026 per Wikipedia. Note scholarship limits are not applicable to House opt-in schools.

rows.statement: Field and Boundary: The wide side (field) and the short side (boundary) of the field, used to align players and calls.

sources.citation: The Pete Kwiatkowski defensive glossary (On3)
sources.quote: The short side of the field is referred to as 'the boundary.'

rows.notes: Single publisher.

rows.statement: field/boundary call: The wide side of the field is 'the field' and the short side is 'the boundary'; defenses set strengths and positions (field corner, boundary corner) by these sides.

sources.citation: The Pete Kwiatkowski defensive glossary (On3)
sources.quote: The wide side is "the field" and the short side is "the boundary."

rows.notes: One publisher (On3, via summariser). Draft framed it as a 'call setting the defensive strength'; the source defines the sides.

rows.statement: field corner: The cornerback who lines up on the wide side of the field (the field), as opposed to the boundary corner on the short side.

sources.citation: The Pete Kwiatkowski defensive glossary (On3)
sources.quote: Field cornerback (C): the most specialized and strictly coverage player on the team

rows.notes: One publisher (On3 Kwiatkowski glossary, via summariser). Draft was right.

rows.statement: Field goal distance: Distance of a field goal attempt: yards from the spot of the kick to the goal line plus the 10-yard end zone, with the kick spot about 7 yards behind the line of scrimmage, so a snap at the 20 is roughly a 37-yard attempt.

sources.citation: Wikipedia: Field goal (gridiron football) (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: the ten yards of the end zone are added to the yard line distance at the spot of the hold.

sources.citation: NFL Rulebook 2026 (NFL Rulebook)
sources.quote: a potential holder and potential kicker seven or more yards behind the neutral zone in position for a place kick

sources.citation: NFL Football Operations: Football Terms (NFL)
sources.quote: snapped from the 15-yardline for the attempt and the kick is equivalent to about a 33-yard field goal

rows.notes: The 37-yard example is my arithmetic (20 + 10 + 7). NFL ops gives about 33 for a snap at the 15, which is consistent with a holder 7 to 8 yards back (Wikipedia positions page: holder 7-8 yards).

rows.statement: Field goal operation: The whole snap, hold and kick sequence of a field goal or extra point, which units time and drill to keep quick.

sources.citation: Special Teams Unit – Field Goals: Operation Times, Working with the Snapper and Holder (Kicking System)
sources.quote: start his approach when the ball is halfway between the snapper and holder to ensure a good get-off time

sources.citation: Special Teams in Football Explained (UA Playbooks) (Under Armour)
sources.quote: On a field goal attempt, the holder is the person who receives the football from the long snapper.

rows.notes: Thinly sourced: no page defines 'operation' as a unit; the Kicking System page is titled around operation times and the snapper-holder-kicker sequence. See Operation time.

rows.statement: Field goal percentage: The percentage of field goal attempts that are made.

sources.citation: CFBTrack: College Football Special Teams Glossary (CFBTrack)
sources.quote: The percentage of field goal attempts that are made.

rows.notes: Renamed from 'Kicker accuracy'. One publisher only.

rows.statement: Field goal range: The distance from which a kicker can reasonably score; about 45 yards at the professional level, per Wikipedia.

sources.citation: Wikipedia: Field goal (gridiron football) (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: within kicking range of the goalposts

sources.citation: NFL Football Operations: Football Terms (NFL)
sources.quote: too far away from the goalposts to attempt a field goal

rows.notes: Thinly sourced; no page gives a hard threshold.

rows.statement: Field position: How far a team is from scoring or where its possession starts; kicking plays are used to improve it.

sources.citation: Wikipedia: Glossary of American football (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: A relative measure of how many yards a team must travel in order to score.

sources.citation: CFBTrack: College Football Special Teams Glossary (CFBTrack)
sources.quote: The average yard line where a team's drives begin.

sources.citation: ITP Glossary: Punt (Inside the Pylon / The Scouting Academy)
sources.quote: to gain superior field position on the opponent’s next possession

rows.notes: Draft said every yard has an expected-point value; the ESPN page on expected points was not opened, so that claim is dropped.

rows.statement: invert: A coverage where a safety drops underneath into the box while a corner plays the deep half, the reverse of normal roles.

sources.quote: Dropping one or both safeties into the box at the snap.

sources.citation: Nick Saban's Cover 7 Defense Explained (Weekly Spiral)

rows.notes: Absorbs draft row 'Cover 2 Invert'. Two publishers.

rows.statement: Jack: A linebacker name whose meaning depends on the system. Most sources use it for the 3-4 outside linebacker or end who is the primary edge pass rusher and may line up on either side; Bowen and the Wikipedia glossary use it for the weak-side inside linebacker of a 3-4.

sources.citation: 3-4 defense (Wikipedia) (Wikipedia)
Linebacker (Wikipedia) (Wikipedia)
The Pete Kwiatkowski defensive glossary (On3)
sources.quote: Jack edge (J): an edge player on the wide side who is a firm run defender and may slide inside

sources.citation: Glossary of American football terms (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: Interior linebacker (ILB) of the 3–4 formation, that plays in the weak side of the formation. Also known as "Mo".

sources.citation: NFL 101: The Basics of the 3-4 Defensive Front (Bleacher Report)
sources.quote: Inside, your two linebackers (Mike/Jack) should have the size to get downhill

sources.citation: A brief introduction to NFL defences (The42)
sources.quote: Jack: The 'other' linebacker in a 4-3 defence.

rows.statement: Jailbreak screen: A wide receiver screen where the linemen sprint out in front of the receiver as blockers.

sources.citation: Screen pass - Wikipedia (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: The wide receiver screen (or "jailbreak screen") is where the linemen sprint out in front of the wide receiver

rows.notes: Single source.

rows.statement: jam: Using the hands to make contact with a receiver and disrupt his route at the line of scrimmage.

sources.citation: Understanding Football with Joel Klatt: Breaking down defensive coverages (FOX Sports)
sources.quote: a defender uses their hands to make contact with the wide receiver and disrupt their route

sources.citation: Cornerback (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: trying to disrupt the receiver's route at the line of scrimmage

sources.citation: The Pete Kwiatkowski defensive glossary (On3)
sources.quote: he needs to be able to jam up

rows.statement: Jammer: A punt-return player who lines up across from a gunner and tries to slow or block him at the line so the returner has more time.

sources.citation: Wikipedia: Gunner (American football) (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: called the jammer, who is assigned to block the gunner of the punting team

sources.citation: Football 101: Special Teams Nomenclature (Steelers Depot)
sources.quote: Defenders who line up opposite of the gunners.

sources.citation: Special Teams in Football Explained (UA Playbooks) (Under Armour)
sources.quote: Jammers are defenders who try to slow down the gunners.

sources.citation: Specialists Week - Gunner vs Vise (PFF)
sources.quote: teams will often use two players opposite each gunner in order to protect against both an inside and outside release

rows.notes: Merged the draft's 'Vice' and 'Jammer' rows: PFF's 'vise' is the same job as jammer (the player opposite the gunner). 'Press man' alias unsourced and left only as a drafted alias. PFF says a vise may get away with more contact than a cornerback.

rows.statement: Jerk: A shallow crossing route with a stutter step.

sources.citation: Route (gridiron football) (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: In essence, it is a shallow crossing route with a stutter step.

rows.notes: Only Wikipedia found. Draft's 'to isolate a linebacker' not in the text I read; removed. Flag: single publisher.

rows.statement: Joint practices: Practice sessions in which two clubs train together, often before a preseason game; under the media policy they must be fully open to local media.

sources.citation: NFL Media Access Policy (2026), hosted by PFWA (NFL (Media Access Policy via PFWA))
sources.quote: If a club conducts joint workouts with another club, those practice sessions must be open in their entirety

sources.citation: Training camp (NFL) - Wikipedia (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: two teams hold a short joint camp and scrimmage at a neutral site in addition to their main camp

rows.statement: Joker: A stand-up end or strong-side linebacker who rushes the passer; Fox also notes it can describe a tight end as a moveable chess piece.

sources.citation: Draft lingo is a special language (Fox Sports)
sources.quote: usually refers to a stand-up defensive end or strong-side linebacker who rushes the passer

rows.notes: Single publisher (Fox).

rows.statement: Jumbo: A short-yardage or goal-line package that adds extra tight ends and backs (or other big bodies) in place of receivers.

sources.citation: Glossary of American football (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: An offensive package which includes two tight ends, a full back and a half back.

sources.citation: Breaking Down NFL Offensive Personnel Groupings (Erik Frenz) (Bleacher Report)

rows.statement: junior college: A two-year college; players can start there and move to a four-year school, and time at one counts toward NCAA eligibility under the pre-2026 rules (and full-time enrollment there starts the new five-year clock).

sources.citation: College Football Recruiting & Roster Glossary (CFBTrack)
sources.quote: A player transferring from a junior college program.

sources.citation: Division I and II Age-Based Eligibility Rules (Eligibility 101) (NCAA)

rows.notes: Wording tightened; 'players develop there' was draft-only. NCAA: full-time enrollment at a two-year college starts the five-year clock.

rows.statement: Just a guy: An ordinary player with no standout trait, not expected to be more than average at his level.

sources.citation: Mayockisms: A glossary of Mike Mayock terms (NFL)
sources.quote: J.A.G.: Just A Guy.

sources.citation: NFL draft glossary: Fluid hips, cow on ice and more (ESPN)
sources.quote: you have been deemed Just A Guy

sources.citation: From Camp Body to Big Bubble to Wood-Toter's Ass: A Scouting Terms Glossary (Defector)
sources.quote: a prospect who does not stand out athletically in any meaningful way

sources.citation: Draft lingo is a special language (Fox Sports)
sources.quote: A JAG is a derogatory term for an average player, or in other words, "just a guy."

rows.statement: K-Gun: The Buffalo Bills' full-time hurry-up, no-huddle offense of the early 1990s, named for tight end Keith McKeller.

sources.citation: Hurry-up offense (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: the most famous and complete hurry-up offense in football

rows.notes: Wikipedia says people assume the K stands for QB Jim Kelly but it was McKeller's nickname 'Killer'. Only one publisher found. Flag: single publisher.

rows.statement: Kamikaze (kickoff coverage): A kickoff-coverage player who starts farther back, gets a running start and attacks the ball carrier with no lane responsibility.

sources.citation: Stop 'Em Cold on Kickoff Returns (Gridiron Strategies)
sources.quote: They align farther behind the ball, get a run at the line of scrimmage and attack the ball carrier.

sources.citation: Wikipedia: Gunner (American football) (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: a gunner, also known as a shooter, flyer, headhunter, or kamikaze

rows.notes: Added. Wikipedia lists 'kamikaze' as an alias of gunner; Gridiron Strategies uses it for a kickoff-coverage role. Two publishers.

rows.statement: Kick return touchdown: A touchdown scored by returning a kickoff or punt.

sources.citation: Wikipedia: Glossary of American football (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: the return of a kickoff or punt for a touchdown

sources.citation: Special Teams in Football Explained (UA Playbooks) (Under Armour)
sources.quote: when the returner catches the football and runs it into the end zone for a score

rows.notes: Two publishers. Wikipedia's glossary folds this into the term 'kick six', which also covers blocked-kick returns.

rows.statement: Kick returner: The specialist who catches a kickoff or punt and runs it back; many teams use one player for both, others split kickoff and punt returners.

sources.citation: Wikipedia: American football positions (special teams) (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: Return specialists are responsible for catching kicked balls (either on kickoffs or punts) and running the ball back.

sources.citation: NFL Football Operations: Football Terms (NFL)
sources.quote: these players catch the football after his opponent punts or kicks off and then attempts to run the ball

sources.citation: Special Teams in Football Explained (UA Playbooks) (Under Armour)
sources.quote: Their primary job is to catch and run back punts and kickoffs.

sources.citation: Wikipedia: Glossary of American football (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: A player on the receiving team who specializes in fielding kicks and running them back.

rows.notes: Merged the draft's 'Return man' row.

rows.statement: Kick six: A touchdown scored by returning a missed or blocked field goal (or a blocked punt, or a kickoff or punt) for a touchdown.

sources.citation: Wikipedia: Glossary of American football (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: A field goal or punt that is blocked and returned for a touchdown

sources.citation: CFBTrack: College Football Special Teams Glossary (CFBTrack)
sources.quote: A touchdown scored by returning a missed or blocked field goal attempt.

rows.notes: Added. The two pages define it slightly differently; Wikipedia's is broader.

rows.statement: Kicker's restraining line: The line the kicker's kicking foot may not pass when the ball is kicked: the kicking team's 35-yard line on a kickoff and its 20-yard line on a safety kick, unless moved by a penalty.

sources.citation: NFL Rulebook 2026 (NFL Rulebook)
sources.quote: the restraining line for the kick by the kicking team shall be its 35-yard line for a kickoff

sources.citation: NCAA Football Rules and Interpretations 2026 (NCAA Rulebook)
sources.quote: Unless relocated by a penalty, the kicking team’s restraining line on a kickoff shall be its 35-yard line

sources.citation: 2024 NFL Season: Explaining rules for new dynamic kickoff (NFL)
sources.quote: The ball will still be kicked from the 35-yard line.

rows.notes: In the NFL the kicker has his own line (6-1-2-a); the other ten kicking-team players use a different line (receiving 40).

rows.statement: Kicking team alignment on kickoff: The legal pre-kick formation: in the NFL the kicker plus ten players with a front foot on the receiving 40, with at least two players in each of three bands across the field; in the NCAA at least four kicking-team players on each side of the kicker.

sources.citation: NFL Rulebook 2026 (NFL Rulebook)
sources.quote: must be lined up with their front foot on the kicking team’s restraining line

sources.citation: NCAA Football Rules and Interpretations 2026 (NCAA Rulebook)
sources.quote: At least four Team A players must be on each side of the kicker

sources.citation: 2024 NFL Season: Explaining rules for new dynamic kickoff (NFL)
sources.quote: None of these players are permitted to move until the ball hits the ground

rows.notes: Draft said minimum players in each field third; the rulebook (6-1-3-a-2) says at least two between sideline and number, two between number and inbounds line, and two inside the inbounds lines. Level is both because the NCAA has its own formation rule (6-1-2-c).

rows.statement: Kicking team's restraining line: The line at the receiving team's 40-yard line on which the ten kicking-team players other than the kicker set their front foot on an NFL kickoff.

sources.citation: NFL Rulebook 2026 (NFL Rulebook)
sources.quote: the restraining line for the remaining 10 players of the kicking team shall be the receiving team’s 40-yard line

sources.citation: 2024 NFL Season: Explaining rules for new dynamic kickoff (NFL)
sources.quote: must line up with one foot on the opponent's 40-yard line

rows.notes: Two sources (rulebook plus NFL.com). In NCAA rule 6-1-1 the kicking team's restraining line is the kicker's line (35), so the phrase means something different at college level.

rows.statement: Kicking tee: The league-approved device that holds the ball for a free kick; it may not raise the ball more than one inch off the ground, and tees are not allowed on field goals or tries.

sources.citation: NFL Rulebook 2026 (NFL Rulebook)
sources.quote: a manufactured tee designed to hold the ball no more than one inch from the ground

sources.citation: NCAA Football Rules and Interpretations 2026 (NCAA Rulebook)
sources.quote: It may not elevate the ball’s lowest point more than one inch above the ground

sources.citation: NFL Football Operations: Football Terms (NFL)
sources.quote: A kick when a football is held stationary and upright, either by the "holder" or by a tee.

rows.notes: NFL 11-4-4 and 11-3-2 bar a tee on a field goal or try kick; NCAA 2-16-4-d forbids a device on a scrimmage place kick.

rows.statement: Kickoff return: A runback after receiving a kickoff.

sources.citation: CFBTrack: College Football Special Teams Glossary (CFBTrack)
sources.quote: A return attempt after receiving a kickoff.

sources.citation: NFL Football Operations: Football Terms (NFL)
sources.quote: these players catch the football after his opponent punts or kicks off and then attempts to run the ball

rows.notes: Renamed from 'Free kick return'; no page used that phrase. Two publishers.

rows.statement: Kickoff safety: The deep kickoff-coverage player, often the kicker, who is the last defender if the returner breaks through the first wave.

sources.citation: Stop 'Em Cold on Kickoff Returns (Gridiron Strategies)
sources.quote: Puts the ball where it is supposed to be, then acts as a safety in case of a coverage breakdown.

rows.notes: Draft term was 'Safety (kickoff last man)'. Only one source found; aliases 'safety man' and 'last man' are drafted, not found. Thinly sourced.

rows.statement: Kickoff specialist: A kicker used only on kickoffs.

sources.citation: Wikipedia: American football positions (special teams) (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: Kickoff specialists are kickers used exclusively on kickoffs.

rows.notes: Added; one publisher.

rows.statement: Kickoff touchback: A kickoff that ends dead in or behind the receiving team's end zone; in the 2026 NFL rulebook the ball is spotted at the 20 if the kick touched the ground or a player in the landing zone first and otherwise at the 35, and in the NCAA at the 25.

sources.citation: NFL Rulebook 2026 (NFL Rulebook)
sources.quote: the dead ball spot is the 35-yard line if, without first touching the ground or a player

sources.citation: NCAA Football Rules and Interpretations 2026 (NCAA Rulebook)
sources.quote: in which case the ball belongs to Team B at its 25-yard line

sources.citation: 2024 NFL Season: Explaining rules for new dynamic kickoff (NFL)
sources.quote: it will be considered a touchback but will bring the ball to out to the 30-yard line

sources.citation: Wikipedia: Kickoff (gridiron football) (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: a touchback, which may occur if the ball is kicked into the receiving team's end zone

rows.notes: Spot differs by source year: NFL.com (2024) says 30; the 2026 rulebook says 35 (20 if the kick landed in the landing zone first). Under Armour and the NFL ops glossary list 25, Dictionary.com lists 35; those pages are older or loose. The 2026 rulebook is the authority.

rows.statement: Kickslide: A 45-degree slide step offensive tackles use off the snap in pass protection.

sources.citation: Kozora football terminology glossary (Steelers Depot, 2013) (Steelers Depot)
sources.quote: 45 degree slide offensive tackles use off the snap.

rows.notes: Only Steelers Depot found. Flag: single publisher.

American Football Terms Glossary | Under Armour (Under Armour (UA Playbooks))
Glossary of Football Terms | ACTIVE.com (ACTIVE.com (Active Network))

sources.quote: a quarterback kneel, also called taking a knee, genuflect offense, kneel-down offense, or victory formation, occurs when the quarterback touches

sources.quote: (e) The "landing zone" shall be the area from the receiving team's 20-yard line extending to its goal line.

Up to two receivers may stand in it before the kick. | Other batch definition: On a kickoff or safety kick, the area from the receiving team's 20-yard line to its goal line; a kick that first touches the ground in advance of its front yard line is a foul if the kicking team does it and it decides whether the ball must be returned.

sources.quote: They have no lane responsibility, they just go!

rows.notes: One high-school-level coaching article; the 'lane integrity' alias is unsourced and kept only as a drafted alias. Thinly sourced.

sources.citation: American Football Terms Glossary | Under Armour (Under Armour (UA Playbooks))

sources.citation: Glossary of Football Terms | ACTIVE.com (ACTIVE.com (Active Network))

sources.quote: length (height and arms) and 40 speed

sources.quote: Arm length is often an important point of discussion when it comes to offensive line and defensive line prospects

sources.quote: his length affects the passer

sources.quote: has long arms, big hands, and outstanding concentration

rows.statement: Leo: A hybrid defensive end/outside linebacker in the Seahawks-style 4-3 Under who rushes from the weak side, usually standing up, in a one-gap technique.

sources.quote: USF a leo

sources.citation: Football terms glossary (NFL)

sources.citation: Linebacker (Wikipedia) (Wikipedia)

rows.statement: linebacker blitz: A blitz by a linebacker, the most common kind.

sources.citation: Blitz (American football) (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: The most common blitzes

rows.notes: Single publisher; quote is the fragment the fetch tool tied to linebacker blitzes.

rows.statement: Long speed: Top running speed over a long distance (straight-line speed), as opposed to quickness over a few steps.

sources.citation: Glossary of American football terms (Wikipedia)

rows.statement: Offset I: An I formation in which the fullback lines up to one side of the line between the quarterback and the halfback.
