sources.quote: This formation is commonly called an Offset I.

sources.citation: Glossary of American football (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: the "offset I" (in which the fullback lines up out of line to the left or right of the quarterback

rows.notes: Both Wikipedia: flag single publisher.

rows.statement: Offside on kickoff: A kicking or receiving player past his restraining line when the ball is kicked; five yards in both the NFL and NCAA rulebooks.

sources.citation: NFL Rulebook 2026 (NFL Rulebook)
sources.quote: The kicker is not offside unless his kicking foot is beyond his restraining line when the ball is kicked.

sources.citation: NCAA Football Rules and Interpretations 2026 (NCAA Rulebook)
sources.quote: All Team B players must be behind their restraining line

rows.notes: Only the two rulebooks. NFL penalty text for being beyond the line when the ball is kicked is 'Loss of five yards' (6-1-3).

rows.statement: Okie front: A 3-4 front descended from the 5-2 Oklahoma defense.

sources.citation: 3-4 defense (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: 5–2 Oklahoma defense

sources.citation: KSR Football Glossary: Vol. 7 (On3)
sources.quote: 3-4 Okie front

rows.notes: Weak. Wikipedia only names the original 5-2 Oklahoma; the On3 KSR page says Okie sends both outside linebackers up the field (as summarized by the fetch tool). Viqtory lists 'Tite/Okie' as one heading. Draft's nose-over-center detail was not found.

rows.statement: Okie front: The traditional two-gap 3-4: ends in 5-techniques, nose head-up on the center, inside linebackers over the bubbles.

sources.citation: NFL 101: The Basics of the 3-4 Defensive Front (Bleacher Report)
sources.quote: both defensive ends and the nose tackle using a “2-gap” technique

rows.notes: Added; one publisher.

rows.statement: On3: A recruiting and transfer-tracking media service that publishes rankings, a transfer portal wire and NIL valuations; its Rivals brand publishes the Rivals Industry Ranking.

sources.citation: What is the NCAA transfer portal? Everything you need to know (On3)
sources.quote: The On3 Transfer Portal Wire provides a real-time feed of player activity

sources.citation: Rivals Industry Ratings and Rankings (On3)
sources.quote: Rivals Ratings and Rankings + Rivals Industry Rankings

rows.notes: Both sources are On3's own pages (one publisher). Proper name; flagged low value.

rows.statement: one-gap: A technique where a lineman is responsible for attacking one gap, instead of holding two.

sources.citation: NFL 101: The Basics of the 4-3 Defensive Front (Bleacher Report)
sources.quote: The 4-3 front is a “one-gap” scheme

sources.citation: NFL 101: The Basics of the 3-4 Defensive Front (Bleacher Report)
sources.quote: there are variations of the defense that will use “1-gap” principles

sources.citation: 3-4 defense (Wikipedia) (Wikipedia)
Defensive Line Techniques - The Prototypes (Pro Football Focus)

rows.statement: one-time transfer rule: A 2021 NCAA rule that let an athlete transfer once without sitting out a year; replaced in April 2024 by unlimited immediate-eligibility transfers.

sources.citation: What is the college football transfer portal? When is it? (ESPN)
sources.quote: NCAA shifted to a one-time transfer rule that gave underclassmen immediate eligibility at their new school

sources.citation: What Are the NCAA Transfer Portal Rules? (Sports Illustrated)
sources.quote: Since 2021, a player was allowed a one-time transfer without having to sit out a season

sources.citation: What is the NCAA transfer portal? Everything you need to know (On3)
sources.quote: allowing players to transfer once without having to sit out a year at their new school.

rows.notes: Historical; adopted April 14, 2021 (On3).

rows.statement: Onside kick: A short free kick the kicking team tries to recover; in the NFL it must travel 10 yards unless a receiver touches it first.

sources.citation: NFL Rulebook 2026 (NFL Rulebook)
sources.quote: An onside kick is defined as a free kick that the kicking team attempts to legally recover

sources.citation: American Football Terms Glossary (UA Playbooks) (Under Armour)
sources.quote: purposely tries to kick the ball only 10 yards

sources.citation: Glossary of Football Terms (ACTIVE.com)
sources.quote: When the kicking team attempts to get the ball back during the kickoff by tapping a short kick.

sources.citation: CFBTrack: College Football Special Teams Glossary (CFBTrack)
sources.quote: A short kickoff designed to give the kicking team a chance to recover the ball.

sources.citation: Wikipedia: Onside kick (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: The kicking team may only recover and retain possession of the kicked ball, but not advance it.

sources.citation: NFL 2026 Rulebook Rule 6-1-6 (NFL Rulebook (primary))
sources.quote: At any time during the game, the kicking team may declare an onside kick by notifying the Referee

sources.citation: 2024 NFL Season: Explaining rules for new dynamic kickoff (superseded) (NFL)
sources.quote: Teams are now only permitted to onside kick in the fourth quarter when trailing and must be declared to the

rows.notes: Added. The 2026 NCAA rulebook text I searched does not use the phrase 'onside kick'. | Other batch definition: A kickoff deliberately kicked short so the kicking team can try to recover it; in the 2026 rulebook the kicking team may declare it at any time during the game.

rows.statement: Open-field yards: Rushing yards gained more than 10 yards past the line of scrimmage.

sources.citation: Metrics and definitions (College Football Data) (College Football Data)
sources.quote: Rushing yards gained more than 10 yards beyond the line of scrimmage.

rows.notes: Single source. The Football Outsiders ALY description (Wikipedia) treats 11+ yard runs as the back's credit, which fits.

rows.statement: Open locker room: Reporters' access to speak with players in the locker room; the policy requires open locker room sessions of at least 45 minutes on Wednesday, Thursday and Friday.

sources.citation: NFL Media Access Policy (2026), hosted by PFWA (NFL (Media Access Policy via PFWA))
sources.quote: This includes mandatory open locker room sessions for a minimum of 45 minutes on Wednesday, Thursday, and Friday.

rows.notes: Postgame access opens after a 10-15 minute wait; training and treatment rooms stay off limits.

rows.statement: Open side: The weak side of the formation, away from the tight end.

sources.citation: Kozora football terminology glossary (Steelers Depot, 2013) (Steelers Depot)
sources.quote: Also known as the "open" side.

sources.citation: Glossary of American football (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: When one tight end is used, the side of the field opposite the tight end.

sources.citation: NFL 101: Breaking Down the Basics of the Route Tree (Matt Bowen) (Bleacher Report)
sources.quote: To the open side: stick out, wheel, deep out, corner and fade.

rows.notes: The Steelers Depot quote ties 'open' to the weak side entry; Bleacher Report uses 'open side' in a route context without defining it. Flag: usage only for the third source.

rows.statement: Operation time: The time from the snap to the kick leaving the foot, which units time and drill; one coaching site lists 1.2 to 1.35 seconds for pro field goal kickers.

sources.citation: Special Teams Unit – Field Goals: Operation Times, Working with the Snapper and Holder (Kicking System)
sources.quote: start his approach when the ball is halfway between the snapper and holder to ensure a good get-off time

sources.citation: How-to guide for punters and special teams coaches (USA Football)
sources.quote: 1.3 seconds to catch and release on a normal punt

rows.notes: The abbreviation 'op time' and 'OT' were not found in any page I opened (only the full phrase 'Operation Times' in the Kicking System title). The Kicking System figures for professionals are printed '1.2-135' (a typo). Thinly sourced.

rows.statement: Option route: A route in which the receiver chooses his path after the snap by reading the defender's leverage.

sources.citation: Football pass routes complete guide (Throw Deep Publishing)
sources.quote: An option route is a general term for any pass route that gives the receiver multiple paths to choose from

sources.citation: NFL 101: Breaking Down the Basics of the Route Tree (Bleacher Report)
sources.quote: the option route (break off the defender's leverage)

sources.citation: Run and shoot offense - Wikipedia (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: A lot of the core concepts involved option routes where receivers would make a decision based on the defender.

rows.statement: Option run: A play in which the ball carrier is chosen after the snap by reading a defender, the quarterback choosing to hand off, keep or pitch.

sources.citation: Glossary of American football terms - Wikipedia (Wikipedia)
American Football Terms Glossary | Under Armour (Under Armour (UA Playbooks))
Option offense - Wikipedia (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: the ballcarrier in a true option running play is determined by reading the defensive alignment

rows.statement: OTAs: Ten voluntary offseason practice days that each club may hold during Phase Three of the offseason program, with all coaches on the field and 11-on-11 work allowed but no live contact.

sources.citation: NFL-NFLPA Collective Bargaining Agreement 2020, Article 21 (Offseason Workouts) (NFL-NFLPA CBA)
sources.quote: each Club may conduct a total of ten days of organized team practice activity ("OTAs" or "OTA days")

sources.citation: Offseason Rules (NFLPA) (NFL Players Association)
sources.quote: A maximum of 4 OTA's for the 3rd or 4th week

sources.citation: Training camp (NFL) - Wikipedia (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: officially called organized team activities, or OTAs

sources.citation: NFL Media Access Policy (2026), hosted by PFWA (NFL (Media Access Policy via PFWA))
sources.quote: Clubs must open to the media at least one of every three Organized Team Activity (OTA) days

rows.notes: CBA Art. 21 Sec. 2(c)(iii): max three OTA days in each of the first two weeks of Phase Three, max four in either the third or fourth week (the other week holds the mandatory minicamp). Sec. 5(b): up to 6 hours at the facility and 2 hours on the field on OTA days. Wikipedia's 'late May and early June' timing is approximate; the CBA ties OTAs to Phase Three of a nine-week program that cannot start before the third Monday in April.

rows.statement: Out: A route that breaks hard toward the sideline after a vertical stem (about 10 to 15 yards, depending on the author).

sources.citation: Route (gridiron football) (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: An out route (or down and out or jet route) is a pattern run by a receiver.

sources.citation: NFL 101: Breaking Down the Basics of the Route Tree (Matt Bowen) (Bleacher Report)
sources.quote: Out (5): The out route (or deep out) again breaks between 12 and 15 yards

sources.citation: Understanding The Route Tree In Football (Mike Pina) (vIQtory Sports)
sources.quote: Typically run by running to 10 yards, then breaking off in a flat 90-degree angle towards the sideline.

sources.citation: The Complete Guide to Football Routes (quick out) (Throw Deep Publishing)
sources.quote: The quick out route is a short pass route

rows.notes: Depth disagrees: 10 yards (vIQtory) vs 12-15 (Bleacher Report); Throw Deep only has a 'quick out' (about five yards).

rows.statement: outside eye: Lining up on the outside shoulder of the player across from you; a defender with 'outside leverage' aligns on the outside eye of the receiver.

sources.citation: NFL 101: Introducing the Basics of Cover 1 (Bleacher Report)
sources.quote: align on the outside shoulder (or outside eye) of the receiver

sources.citation: NFL 101: Introducing the Basics of Cover 4 (Bleacher Report)
sources.quote: align off (seven to eight yards) with an outside shade (outside eye)

sources.citation: Defensive Line Techniques & Gap Identification (Lancer Reisland (Substack))

rows.notes: Used for both linemen and defensive backs. 'eye' and 'shoulder' are used interchangeably in Bowen's pieces.

rows.statement: outside leverage: Lining up on the outside shoulder of the receiver to force him inside.

sources.citation: Football Terms (The Daily Wildcat) (The Daily Wildcat)
sources.quote: stay on the outside shoulder of the receiver and force him into the middle

rows.notes: Single publisher; the term 'outside leverage' itself appears in Weekly Spiral for the Cone call.

rows.statement: outside linebacker: A linebacker aligned outside the box tackles: responsible for outside containment, blitzing and covering the flats; in a 3-4 he is often the main edge rusher.

sources.citation: Linebacker (Wikipedia) (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: usually responsible for outside containment

sources.citation: A brief introduction to NFL defences (The42)
sources.quote: the strong side linebacker lines up on the same side of the field as the offence's tight end

sources.citation: Glossary of American football terms (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: In a 3–4 formation, an OLB may be designated as a "rush linebacker", rushing the passer on almost every play

sources.citation: NFL 101: The Basics of the 3-4 Defensive Front (Bleacher Report)
sources.quote: the two outside linebackers (the premium position in the 3-4) make plays as edge defenders

rows.statement: Outside zone: A zone run that stretches the defense laterally toward the edge, also called a stretch play, with the lanes read by the runner.

sources.citation: Breaking down PFF's run concepts (PFF)
sources.quote: Also known as a “stretch” play, the outside zone play is designed to get the defense moving laterally

sources.citation: Blocking (American football) (zone play types) (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: zone plays are categorized as Inside Zone, Outside Zone, and Stretch

rows.notes: Draft detail 'one cut after reading the edge defender' is not in the sources read; removed. Wikipedia text is a paraphrase from my read, not exact quote; weakest of the two. Two publishers.

rows.statement: Over front: A 4-3 front shifted to the strong (tight end, closed) side: the 3-technique tackle lines up on the strong side and the nose on the weak side in a 0 shade or 2i.

sources.citation: NFL 101: The Basics of the 4-3 Defensive Front (Bleacher Report)
sources.quote: In the “Over” front, the “3-technique” defensive tackle is aligned to the closed side of the formation (tight end side)

rows.notes: One publisher (Bleacher Report/Bowen). Wikipedia 4-3 page (via summariser) does not define it.

rows.statement: Overachiever: A player with limited athleticism who is productive through work ethic and intangibles; the underachiever has more talent than output.

sources.citation: From Camp Body to Big Bubble to Wood-Toter's Ass: A Scouting Terms Glossary (Defector)
sources.quote: An overachiever is a player who has limited athleticism but is really productive because of his work ethic and intangibles.

rows.notes: Single publisher (Defector).

rows.statement: Overtime coin toss: A separate coin toss at the start of overtime; the winner chooses between receiving or kicking and which goal to defend.

sources.citation: NFL 2026 Rulebook Rule 16-1-2 (NFL Rulebook (primary))
sources.quote: the Referee shall immediately toss a coin at the center of the field

rows.notes: Second quote concerns the third postseason overtime period. Another toss occurs at the end of a fourth overtime period (16-1-4(i)). Rulebook only.

rows.statement: owner: The person or family that owns the franchise; top football executives such as the general manager report to the owner or chairman.

sources.citation: What Exactly Does Each Member of an NFL Team's Front Office Do? (Bleacher Report)
sources.quote: He answers directly to the owner and has final veto power on all player-related decisions the team makes.

sources.citation: NFL draft board building 101: Inside the secretive yearlong grind (ESPN)
sources.quote: Titans controlling owner Amy Adams Strunk

sources.citation: Chiefs Front Office Staff (NFL (Kansas City Chiefs club site))
sources.quote: reporting directly to Chiefs Chairman and CEO Clark Hunt

rows.notes: Draft's 'hires top executives' only partly shown (GM hires head coach, BR).

rows.statement: Pad level: How low a player keeps his shoulder pads; staying low wins leverage and playing too upright loses it.

sources.citation: 2018 Scouting Glossary (Draft Insiders)
sources.quote: Loses leverage by playing too upright.

sources.citation: Draft lingo is a special language (Fox Sports)
sources.quote: Defensive linemen who are too upright often receive this moniker.

sources.citation: How Do Scouts Break Down NFL Offensive Line Prospects? (Bleacher Report)
sources.quote: Does the lineman maintain good posture and leverage throughout the block?

rows.statement: Padded practice: A practice in which players are required to wear helmets and shoulder pads in addition to any other club-required gear; the CBA caps how many a club may hold.

sources.citation: NFL-NFLPA Collective Bargaining Agreement 2020, Article 24 (Regular Season and Postseason Practices) (NFL-NFLPA CBA)
sources.quote: a "padded practice" shall be defined as a practice in which players are required to wear helmets and shoulder pads

rows.notes: Merged the draft row 'Full pads'. Post-acclimation camp: max one padded practice per day, 2.5 on-field hours, no more than three in a row. Regular season: 14 (11 in first eleven weeks, 3 in the last six), one per week in the postseason. QB, kicker, punter, long snapper helmet/pad wear by choice does not make it a padded practice (Art. 23 Sec. 7(e)).

rows.statement: Palms: A split-field coverage from a Cover 2 look where the corner reads the number-two receiver's release and jumps the first outside route, with a safety deep over the top; also called 2-Trap.

sources.citation: Fantasy shells: coverage glossary (Fantasy Points)
sources.quote: Also referred to as 2-Trap, this is a variant of Cover 2.

sources.citation: Football Plays: defensive coverages (CFBTrack)
sources.quote: A split-field coverage where the corner and safety read the No. 2 receiver

sources.citation: NFL 101: Introducing Trap Coverage (Bleacher Report)
sources.quote: trap coverages have different terminology, such as “gold,” “2-Trap” or “Kathy.”

sources.citation: The Complete Defensive Coverage Guide (Viqtory Sports)
sources.quote: palms coverage is how defenses will protect themselves against offenses that throw flat or bubble routes

rows.notes: Draft said 'quarters rules'; sources describe a Cover 2 variant (trap) with the corner reading No. 2.

rows.statement: Pancake block: A block that hits the defender so hard he is driven to the ground.

sources.citation: Glossary of American football (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: A "pancake block"; sometimes shortened to "cake"; is a particularly effective block where the player being blocked is pushed onto

sources.citation: American Football Terms Glossary (Under Armour)
sources.quote: When a blocker for the ball carrier hits or pushes a would-be tackler especially hard and brings them to the

rows.notes: Draft said 'puts defender on his back'; Under Armour says 'brings them to the ground'.

rows.statement: pass defense: Defending against passing plays through coverage and pass rush.

sources.citation: Football terms: pass defenses (Daily Wildcat)
sources.quote: Primarily responsible for pass coverage defense.

sources.citation: Glossary of American football terms (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: Primarily responsible for pass coverage defense.

rows.notes: Generic phrase; no formal entry. Weak.

rows.statement: Pass protection (running back): A back's ability to block rushers and pick up blitzes to protect the quarterback.

sources.citation: A Four-Step Guide to Watching Football Like a Scout (The Ringer)
sources.quote: Can he pass-protect? Can he catch passes?

rows.notes: Only a checklist mention found (Norris, in Ringer 2017). Single source, no definition sentence.

rows.statement: pass rush: The defenders' effort to reach and pressure the quarterback on a pass play, usually by the four down linemen plus any blitzers.

sources.citation: Glossary of American football terms (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: principal function is to deliver pressure to the quarterback

sources.citation: College Football Defense Glossary (CFBTrack)
sources.quote: Pressure: A pass-rush event that disrupts the quarterback, including sacks, hits, hurries, or forced movement.

sources.citation: NFL 101: Introducing the Basics of Cover 2 (Bleacher Report)

rows.notes: Generic term; no formal definition line.

rows.statement: pass strength: The side of the formation with the most passing threats, where the defense adds a coverage player.

sources.citation: Unlocking the Fangio Coverage System (MatchQuarters) (MatchQuarters (Cody Alexander))
sources.quote: play with an extra coverage defender to the passing strength.

sources.citation: How to understand Nick Saban's pattern match cover-3 defense (USA Football)
sources.quote: goes to the passing strength of the formation

sources.citation: Understanding Football with Joel Klatt: Breaking down defensive coverages (FOX Sports)
sources.quote: The safety goes to the side of the wide receiver, the passing strength.

rows.statement: Passing down: A down with enough yardage to go that the offense is expected to pass: second-and-7 or 8 and longer, or third or fourth down with 5 or more yards.

sources.citation: College football advanced stats glossary (Football Study Hall) (Football Study Hall (SB Nation))
sources.quote: Second-and-7 or more, third-and-5 or more, or fourth-and-5 or more.

sources.citation: Metrics and definitions (College Football Data) (College Football Data)
sources.quote: classify second-and-8 or longer and third- or fourth-and-5 or longer as passing downs.

rows.notes: Added; companion of Standard down.

rows.statement: pattern match: A zone-looking coverage in which defenders switch to man-style responsibilities based on how the receivers' routes develop.

sources.citation: College Football Defense Glossary (CFBTrack)
sources.quote: A hybrid coverage that starts like zone but turns into man-like responsibilities based on route patterns.

sources.citation: NFL 101: Introducing the Basics of Cover 4 (Bleacher Report)
sources.quote: pattern match the vertical release from No. 1 in the outside 1/4

sources.citation: A fan's guide to modern NFL coverages (zonecoverage.com)

rows.notes: Added.

rows.statement: Pavia ruling: A December 2024 federal preliminary injunction for former JUCO player Diego Pavia on how the NCAA counts non-NCAA seasons toward eligibility; the NCAA then gave a blanket extra year for 2025-26.

sources.citation: Redshirt (college sports) (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: a U.S. District Court issued a preliminary injunction in favor of Diego Pavia (former JUCO player)

rows.notes: Draft called it a court case; Wikipedia describes a preliminary injunction. Single publisher; flagged.

rows.statement: pay-for-play: Paying athletes directly for playing or to recruit them; the NCAA long banned it, and revenue sharing since July 2025 lets schools pay players directly.

sources.citation: What is the college football transfer portal? When is it? (ESPN)
sources.quote: While the NCAA has always prohibited pay-for-play recruiting and the use of NIL deals as inducements

sources.citation: How athletes will be paid as July 1 ushers in new era for college sports (CBS Sports)
sources.quote: For the first time, schools can directly pay players for performance.

rows.notes: Draft said 'partly allowed through revenue sharing'; CBS says direct pay for performance is allowed for opt-in schools.

rows.statement: pedal: A defender moving backward with short, quick steps while keeping his eyes on the receiver or quarterback.

sources.citation: NFL 101: Introducing the Basics of Cover 3 (Bleacher Report)
sources.quote: before getting into his pedal to maintain the cushion versus the receiver

sources.citation: NFL 101: Introducing the Basics of Cover 1 (Bleacher Report)
sources.quote: Defenders will not get into their backpedal until the receiver has cleared the three-step concepts

rows.notes: One publisher (Bowen).

rows.statement: penetrate: To charge through a gap into the backfield with speed and quickness to disrupt the play, as the 3-technique and rush end do in a 4-3.

sources.citation: NFL 101: The Basics of the 3-4 Defensive Front (Bleacher Report)
sources.quote: aren’t built to use speed/quickness to penetrate the gaps/edges of the line

sources.citation: The glossary: Explaining the different defensive line techniques and associated responsibilities (neworleans.football)
Defensive Line Techniques - The Prototypes (Pro Football Focus)

rows.notes: Meaning by usage; no glossary line found.

rows.statement: Period extension: One extra untimed down given at the end of a period or half when the defense commits an accepted live-ball foul on the last play, among other cases.

sources.citation: NFL 2026 Rulebook Rule 4-8-2 (NFL Rulebook (primary))
sources.quote: A period may be extended for one untimed down, if any of the following occurs

rows.notes: Rulebook only (WG has a navbox link 'Untimed play' but no definition read).

rows.statement: Personnel grouping: A two-digit shorthand for the offense's skill players on the field: the first digit is the number of running backs and the second is the number of tight ends, with the rest of the five eligible spots being wide receivers.

sources.citation: Football 101: Personnel Groupings (Steelers Depot, 2020) (Steelers Depot)
sources.quote: The first number tells you the backs, the second the tight ends.

sources.citation: Breaking Down NFL Offensive Personnel Groupings (Erik Frenz) (Bleacher Report)
sources.quote: The first number is the number of running backs, and the second is the number of tight ends.

sources.citation: Football 101 | Daily Brew (Houston Texans) (Houston Texans)
sources.quote: The first digit is the number of running backs on the field.

sources.citation: Personnel grouping (gridiron football) (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: a specific number system is used to refer to the number of running backs and tight ends on the field

rows.notes: All four agree on the digit rule. Wide receivers are the remainder of the five eligibles (inferred from 10 personnel = four receivers in Steelers Depot).

rows.statement: Pete Carroll defense: The 4-3 Under, Leo end and Cover 3 with a safety dropping near linebacker depth, put together by Pete Carroll and Dan Quinn at Seattle.

sources.citation: Seattle 4-3 hybrid defense (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: a Cover 3 defensive backfield where a safety comes down to about linebacker depth

sources.citation: ITP Glossary: Cover 3 (Inside the Pylon / Scouting Academy)
sources.quote: the Seattle Seahawks rode a modified Cover 3 to the Super Bowl XLVIII Championship

sources.citation: Formation (American football) (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: Seattle Cover 3

rows.notes: Wikipedia credits Carroll and Quinn and the Kiffin 4-3 Under base.

rows.statement: Peter block: A nickname for a low (cut) block used in pass protection.

sources.citation: More than just a pocket: Inside look at NFL pass protections (Nick Shook) (NFL)
sources.quote: My favorite acceptable nickname is Peter block.

rows.notes: NFL.com names it a nickname within its 'going low' discussion (after cut block) but does not define it; meaning inferred. Draft said 'meant to bring the rusher down'. Flag: single publisher, partly inferred.

rows.statement: Phase One: The first two weeks of the nine-week offseason program, limited to strength, conditioning and rehab with no helmets and only strength coaches allowed on the field.

sources.citation: NFL-NFLPA Collective Bargaining Agreement 2020, Article 21 (Offseason Workouts) (NFL-NFLPA CBA)
sources.quote: Phase One shall consist of the first two weeks of the Club's offseason workout program.

sources.citation: Offseason Rules (NFLPA) (NFL Players Association)
sources.quote: Two weeks | Limited to strength and conditioning activities ("dead ball"); only strength and conditioning coaches allowed on field

rows.notes: CBA allows a few exceptions to the dead-ball rule (QBs throwing uncovered, kickers/punters, returners, JUGGS machines). NFLPA page says 90 minutes max on the field and a 4-hour facility cap.

rows.statement: Phase Three: The final four weeks of the offseason program, when the ten OTA days (and the mandatory veteran minicamp) are held; helmets may be required but there is no live contact and no shells.

sources.citation: NFL-NFLPA Collective Bargaining Agreement 2020, Article 21 (Offseason Workouts) (NFL-NFLPA CBA)
sources.quote: Phase Three shall consist of the next four weeks of the Club's offseason workout program.

sources.citation: Offseason Rules (NFLPA) (NFL Players Association)
sources.quote: 7 on 7, 9 on 7 and 11 on 11 drills will be permitted provided no live contact takes place

rows.notes: Team offense vs. team defense is allowed in Phase Three provided no live contact occurs; one-on-one offense vs. defense drills are barred except simulated press coverage using hand placement outside the 10-yard line.

rows.statement: Phase Two: The next three weeks of the offseason program, when all coaches may be on the field for individual and perfect-play drills (offense or defense only), with no offense versus defense work.

sources.citation: NFL-NFLPA Collective Bargaining Agreement 2020, Article 21 (Offseason Workouts) (NFL-NFLPA CBA)
sources.quote: Phase Two shall consist of the next three weeks of the Club's offseason workout program.

sources.citation: Offseason Rules (NFLPA) (NFL Players Association)
sources.quote: No offense vs. defense, no one-on-one, no helmets

rows.notes: CBA permits offense-vs-offense and defense-vs-defense lineups of eleven or fewer at walkthrough pace (the 'Pro Bowl practice pace').

rows.statement: Phone booth: An offensive lineman with below-average feet who is effective only in tight spaces.

sources.citation: Mayockisms: A glossary of Mike Mayock terms (NFL)
sources.quote: An offensive lineman with below-average feet that performs best in short areas.

rows.notes: Single publisher (Mayock via NFL.com).

rows.statement: Pin and pull: An outside-zone technique where linemen pin a backside defender while the next backside lineman pulls around toward the second level.

sources.citation: Blocking (American football) (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: For the outside varieties of the zone play a scheme that is called Pin&Pull has had great success.

rows.notes: Only Wikipedia found. Flag: single publisher.

rows.statement: Pistol: A short-shotgun formation: the quarterback lines up a few yards behind the center and the running back sits directly behind him.

sources.citation: Glossary of American football (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: A hybrid version of the shotgun in which the quarterback lines up about three yards behind the center

sources.citation: Pistol offense (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: the quarterback lines up four yards behind the center

sources.citation: Spread offense (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: take a short shotgun snap

rows.notes: Sources disagree on depth: glossary and Spread offense say about three yards; Pistol offense says four yards (running back three yards behind him). Popularised by Chris Ault at Nevada. All Wikipedia: flag single publisher.

rows.statement: Pitch: A toss from the quarterback to a trailing running back, as on an option play.

sources.citation: NFL Football Operations | Football Terms (NFL Football Operations)
sources.quote: Pitch: A long underhanded toss, usually using both hands, from the quarterback to a running back on running plays.

sources.citation: Option offense - Wikipedia (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: pitch the ball to a trailing running back angling towards the sideline

Wikipedia's two pages count as one publisher. | Other batch definition: The clock-driven offense used near the end of a half, mixing no-huddle tempo with plays that stop the clock, such as sideline passes.

sources.citation: 28 Football Terms to Make You Sound Like a Pro (Dictionary.com)
sources.quote: The two-point attempt a team is allowed to make after scoring a touchdown.

sources.citation: Football Terms (NFL Football Operations) (NFL)
sources.quote: After scoring a touchdown, an offense can opt to run one play from the defense's two-yard line to try to

The NCAA 3-yard quote comes from the extra-period rule text but the same 3-yard try spot is in Rule 8-3-2. | Other batch definition: After a touchdown, one play from the opponent's two-yard line; scoring on it earns two extra points, and the team may choose it instead of kicking.

rows.statement: Under center: The quarterback lines up directly behind the center and takes the snap straight from him.

rows.statement: Under front: A 4-3 front where the nose tackle sits on the closed (tight end) side and the 3-technique to the open side, the opposite of the Over front.

rows.notes: Single definitional source; flagged. CBS shows a school covering unofficial-visit expenses counted as a violation.

sources.quote: The upback, also known as the personal protector, is a blocking back

sources.quote: A player, in a scrimmage kick (punts and field goals) or kneel formations, who lines up behind the offensive line.

rows.statement: Upman: On a kickoff, every receiving-team player except the one or two deep returners.

rows.notes: Added from Wikipedia's glossary (the draft's 'Upback' kickoff meaning). One publisher only; flagged. Draft said upbacks block and may field short kicks; the source says only that all non-returners are upmen.

sources.citation: NCAA Football Rules and Interpretations 2026 (NCAA Rulebook)

rows.notes: The draft said 18 feet 6 inches in the NFL only; the NCAA rulebook gives the same width (Rule 1-2-5, goal). NCAA uprights extend at least 30 feet above the ground. The NFL rulebook describes the 18 ft 6 in as the crossbar length.

sources.quote: Yankee concept is generally a two man deep crossing combo

sources.citation: Football Play Guide: pass concepts (CFBTrack)
sources.quote: A deep over/crosser paired with a vertical clear-out, usually off play-action.

rows.statement: Yards after catch: Yards gained by a receiver after the catch.

sources.citation: NGS Glossary (NFL)
sources.quote: The yards gained after catch by a receiver.

sources.citation: Glossary of American football (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: the amount of yardage gained after initial catch.

sources.citation: West Coast offense (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: allows the receiver to gain the majority of the yards after the catch

rows.notes: Merged from two rows. The Next Gen Stats glossary also defines expected YAC from tracking data.

rows.statement: Yards per route run: Receiving yards divided by the number of pass routes the player ran.

sources.citation: Football analytics definitions (Sumer Sports)
sources.quote: Total receiving yards divided by the number of pass routes the player ran.

sources.citation: PFF Signature Statistics - a glossary (PFF)
sources.quote: takes into account the amount of snaps a receiver runs a route as an eligible receiver.

rows.statement: year in residence: The old rule that a transferring underclassman had to sit out a year at the new school before playing, unless he got an NCAA waiver.

sources.citation: What is the NCAA transfer portal? Everything you need to know (On3)
sources.quote: Players were required to serve a "year in residence" before becoming eligible to play at their new school

sources.citation: What is the college football transfer portal? When is it? (ESPN)
sources.quote: underclassmen transfers were required to sit out a year in residence at their new school

rows.notes: Historical; graduate transfers were exempt (ESPN).

rows.statement: Yellow line: A solid yellow line six feet behind the white border in the bench area; players (except one charting the game) stay behind it, leaving the strip for coaches.

sources.citation: NFL 2026 Rulebook Rule 1-1-2 (NFL Rulebook (primary))
sources.quote: a solid yellow, 8-inch-wide line, six feet behind the solid border will delineate a special area for coaches

rows.notes: Draft said 'limiting coaches' - actually the line marks the coaches' area and keeps players behind it. Rulebook only.

rows.statement: Z receiver: In letter-based systems, the Z is the flanker: the receiver who lines up a yard off the line of scrimmage, usually to the tight end's side.

sources.citation: Deep Dive: A Pro-Style Formation System (Queer Football Breakdowns) (Queer Football Breakdowns)
sources.quote: Flanker/#2 receiver. It usually travels to the same side as the Y.

sources.citation: Glossary of American football (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: A wide receiver who lines up in the backfield outside of another receiver. The term is used infrequently in American

rows.notes: Two publishers.

rows.statement: Zap motion: A motion call telling the Z to start in the called formation, cross to the offside guard and return to his original spot.

sources.citation: Motions and shifts (oocities (coaching notes))
sources.quote: tells the Z to start in the called formation.

rows.notes: Single informal coaching page.

rows.statement: zero blitz: A blitz run out of Cover 0: more rushers than the offense has blockers, every receiver covered man-to-man and no deep safety.

sources.citation: The Blitz in Football: The Complete Guide (Throw Deep Publishing)
sources.quote: it leaves no deep safety covering the deep section of the field

sources.citation: Blitz Guide For New Football Coaches (Viqtory Sports)
sources.quote: the maximum number of defenders are trying to sack the quarterback

sources.citation: Football 101: Basic Defensive Coverages (Steelers Depot)
sources.quote: Cover 0, our first breakdown, means there isn't any deep safety.

sources.citation: Glossary of American football terms (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: Cover zero – strict man-to-man coverage with no help from safeties

rows.statement: zone blitz: A rush of five or more in which one or more players who normally rush (often a lineman or edge) drop into coverage while other defenders rush, behind a zone coverage.

sources.citation: Glossary of American football terms (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: A defensive package combining a blitz with zone-pass coverage.

sources.citation: College Football Defense Glossary (CFBTrack)
sources.quote: A blitz where some traditional pass rushers drop into coverage while other defenders rush.

sources.citation: NFL 101: Breaking Down the Basics of the Zone Blitz (Bleacher Report)
sources.quote: five-man pressure with the protection of a three-deep, three-under zone shell in the back end

sources.citation: Zone blitz (Wikipedia) (Wikipedia)
ITP Glossary: Cover 3 (Inside the Pylon / Scouting Academy)
sources.quote: 3-4 teams often pair their zone blitz concepts with Cover 3

rows.notes: ORIGIN CONFLICT: Wikipedia glossary says it was invented by Dick LeBeau; the Wikipedia Zone blitz article (via summariser) says Bill Arnsparger developed it with the Dolphins in 1971 and LeBeau popularized it in the early 1990s with Pittsburgh. Absorbs the draft row 'Bill Arnsparger zone blitz'. | Other batch definition: A blitz that sends extra rushers but drops some linemen or rushers into zone coverage, so the blitzer is disguised.

rows.statement: Zone blocking: A run-blocking scheme in which linemen block together to create lanes for the runner, with no hole assigned in advance.

sources.citation: Blocking (American football) - Wikipedia (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: Zone blocking is a technique that is a simple and effective scheme for creating lanes for running plays.

sources.citation: Kozora football terminology glossary (Steelers Depot)
sources.quote: a scheme where there is no assigned hole for the running back to run through

sources.citation: Glossary of American football terms - Wikipedia (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: a zone block, which is any block executed in a zone blocking scheme

rows.notes: Draft wording about blocking 'areas rather than defenders' is an inference from these quotes.

rows.statement: zone coverage: Pass coverage in which each defender covers an area of the field rather than a specific receiver.

sources.citation: Glossary of American football terms (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: A defense in which players are in pass-coverage zones of the field, instead of covering individual players.

sources.citation: College Football Defense Glossary (CFBTrack)
sources.quote: Coverage where defenders are responsible for areas of the field.

sources.citation: Football terms: pass defenses (Daily Wildcat)
sources.quote: Each player is designated a "zone" on the field and he is responsible for whatever offensive player enters that area.

sources.citation: The Complete Defensive Coverage Guide (Viqtory Sports)
sources.quote: Each player on the defense has a role or responsibility to cover a certain area on the field

rows.statement: Zone read: A read option run: the line zone-blocks one way while the quarterback reads a defensive end and either hands off or keeps.

sources.citation: Option offense (read option) (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: In a read option play, the quarterback has only one teammate to whom he can pitch or hand the ball

sources.citation: Spread offense (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: Many spread teams use the read option running play to put pressure on both sides of the defense.

rows.notes: All Wikipedia: flag single publisher. Wikipedia says the QB 'reads' the end on the side the play is designed to go.

rows.statement: Zoom motion: A motion call in which the Z starts in the called formation and motions across to the other side.

sources.citation: Motions and Shifts (oocities (theprez98 football notes))
sources.quote: Zoom, which tells the Z to start in the called formation and motion across the formation
